title: Plants in Bhartiya Gyan Parampara
subtitle: Botany, history of botany in India, Vedic concepts, Indian Rishis and traditional plant knowledge.

topics.title: Botany — Definition, Scope and Importance
topics.subtitle: Plant science and its major branches

blocks.title: Definition
blocks.body: Botany is the branch of Biology dealing with the scientific study of plants, including their structure, growth, reproduction, metabolism, diseases and evolutionary relationships. It is also called Plant Biology or Phytology.

topics.diagram: Diagram: branches of Botany / importance of plants.

left.title: Ancient and Medieval
left.body: Rigveda and Atharvaveda described plants; Parashar's Vrikshayurveda and the Charaka and Sushruta traditions contributed to plant knowledge. Mughal-period gardens and horticulture expanded plant use and cultivation.

right.title: British and Modern
right.body: William Roxburgh is described as the Father of Indian Botany and J.D. Hooker compiled Flora of British India. Modern development includes the Botanical Survey of India, CSIR/ICAR research, Green Revolution work and J.C. Bose's studies of plant sensitivity.

topics.title: Botanical Concepts in Vedas, Upanishads, Ramayan and Puranas
topics.subtitle: Traditional classification and plant knowledge

left.title: Vedic concepts
left.body: Rigveda: Vanaspati, Vriksha, Oshadhi and Virudh. Atharvaveda contains extensive references to medicinal plants and the concept of Bheshaj.

right.title: Later texts
right.body: Upanishads discuss plant consciousness. Ramayan mentions Ashoka Vatika, Panchavati and Sanjeevani. Puranic texts describe plant categories and medicinal or sacred plants.

topics.title: Contribution of Indian Rishis
topics.subtitle: Parashar, Charak, Sushrut, Surpaal and Kautilya

left.title: Major contributors
items: Parashar — Vrikshayurveda; plant classification and diseases
Charak — medicinal plant groups and Dravyaguna
Sushrut — medicinal plants and plant-based surgical materials

right.title: Other contributions
items: Surpaal — horticulture, propagation and crop improvement
Kautilya — economic plants, forest conservation and plant medicines

title: Morphology — External Structure of Plants
subtitle: Thallus and cormus, modifications of roots, stems and leaves, and reproductive external structures.

topics.title: Basic Concepts — Thallus vs Plant Body
topics.subtitle: Lower plant body and differentiated cormus

left.title: Thallus
left.body: Body undivided; root, stem and leaf differentiation absent; vascular tissue absent. Examples include Spirogyra, Ulva and Marchantia.

right.title: Plant Body (Cormus)
right.body: Root, stem and leaf are distinct; vascular tissue is present. Seen in ferns, gymnosperms and angiosperms.

title: Anatomy — Internal Structure of Plants
subtitle: Plant cell, tissues and comparative anatomy of roots, stems and leaves.

blocks.title: Cell Theory
blocks.body: Schleiden (1838), Schwann (1839) and Virchow (1855): “Omnis cellula e cellula”.

left.title: Plant-specific prominence
left.body: Cell wall provides support; chloroplast performs photosynthesis and has its own DNA; the large vacuole maintains turgor and stores materials.

right.title: Other organelles
right.body: Plasma membrane, nucleus, mitochondria, ribosomes, Golgi apparatus and rough/smooth ER perform transport, control, respiration, protein synthesis and packaging functions.

topics.title: Dicot and Monocot Root Anatomy
topics.subtitle: Internal comparison

left.title: Dicot root
left.body: Radial bundles, fewer xylem arms, cambium associated with secondary growth and pith small or absent.

right.title: Monocot root
right.body: Radial polyarch bundles, large distinct pith and no secondary growth.

topics.diagram: Cross-section: dicot root vs monocot root.

topics.title: Dicot and Monocot Stem Anatomy
topics.subtitle: Vascular arrangement and secondary growth

left.title: Dicot stem
left.body: Collenchymatous hypodermis; vascular bundles in a ring, open and collateral; secondary growth possible.

right.title: Monocot stem
right.body: Sclerenchymatous hypodermis; vascular bundles scattered, closed and collateral; secondary growth absent.

topics.diagram: Cross-section: dicot stem vs monocot stem.

topics.title: Leaf Anatomy
topics.subtitle: Dorsiventral and isobilateral leaf structure

left.title: Dorsiventral (dicot)
left.body: Upper epidermis, palisade mesophyll, spongy mesophyll and lower epidermis with abundant stomata.

right.title: Isobilateral (monocot)
right.body: Stomata on both epidermal surfaces; mesophyll generally undifferentiated; Kranz anatomy and bulliform cells are important features in the source notes.

title: General Idea of Plant Physiology
subtitle: Water relations, transpiration, ascent of sap, photosynthesis and respiration.

topics.title: Water Relations
topics.subtitle: Diffusion, osmosis, imbibition and water potential

blocks.title: Water potential
blocks.body: Ψ = Ψs + Ψp. Pure water has Ψ = 0; solutes make water potential negative.

left.title: Key processes
items: Osmosis — water through a semipermeable membrane
Imbibition — water absorption by solid colloids

right.title: Cell states
items: Plasmolysis — membrane shrinks away from wall in hypertonic solution

left.title: Transpiration types
left.body: Stomatal: 80–90%; Cuticular: 10–20%; Lenticular: less than 1% in the source notes.

right.title: Cohesion-Tension Theory
right.body: Dixon and Joly (1894): transpiration creates tension in xylem; cohesion and adhesion maintain a continuous water column from roots to leaves.

topics.title: Photosynthesis
topics.subtitle: Light reactions, Calvin cycle, C4 and CAM

left.title: Light and C3 reactions
left.body: Light reactions occur in thylakoid membranes and form ATP/NADPH with O₂ release. The Calvin cycle occurs in the stroma and fixes CO₂ through RuBP/Rubisco.

right.title: C4 and CAM
right.body: C4 plants use mesophyll and bundle sheath with OAA as first product. CAM plants open stomata mainly at night and store CO₂ as malic acid.

topics.diagram: Chloroplast with grana and stroma; pathway flow.

topics.title: Respiration
topics.subtitle: Glycolysis, pyruvate oxidation, Krebs cycle and ETC

right.title: ETC and RQ
right.body: Oxidative phosphorylation occurs on the inner mitochondrial membrane and is listed as 32–34 ATP. RQ = CO₂ released / O₂ absorbed.

topics.title: Physiology Integration
topics.subtitle: Linking water, transport, photosynthesis and respiration

blocks.title: Core revision logic
blocks.body: Water enters and moves through the plant; transpiration drives the water column; photosynthesis captures energy and forms carbohydrates; respiration releases usable energy as ATP.

topics.diagram: Concept map connecting all Unit IV processes.

title: Plant Reproduction, Growth and Propagation
subtitle: Propagules, sexual and asexual reproduction, hormones, elicitors and alternation of generations.

left.title: Natural propagules
left.body: Rhizome, tuber, bulb, corm, runner, sucker, bulbil and foliar buds are listed with examples such as ginger, potato, onion, banana, Agave and Bryophyllum.

right.title: Artificial methods
right.body: Cutting uses a stem/leaf/root piece; grafting joins stock and scion. Examples in the source include rose, hibiscus, begonia, mango and apple.

blocks.title: Double fertilization
blocks.body: Sperm + egg → zygote (2n) → embryo; second sperm + two polar nuclei → endosperm (3n). The source notes identify this as unique to angiosperms and credit Nawaschin (1898).

topics.title: Plant Hormones and Role of Elicitors
topics.subtitle: Growth regulators and defence signalling

right.title: Elicitors
right.body: Biotic or abiotic signals such as pathogen factors, UV, heat or wounding can trigger defence, secondary metabolites and systemic acquired resistance (SAR).

topics.diagram: Hormone action chart / defence signalling flow.

topics.title: Gametophyte and Sporophyte
topics.subtitle: Dominant phases in major plant groups

left.title: Groups
left.body: Algae and bryophytes have a prominent gametophyte phase in the source table, while pteridophytes, gymnosperms and angiosperms are described with dominant sporophytes.

right.title: Reduction of gametophyte
right.body: In seed plants the gametophytes are highly reduced, represented by structures such as pollen and embryo sac.

topics.diagram: Compare dominant phase across plant groups.

topics.title: Alternation of Generations
topics.subtitle: Cycle between haploid and diploid phases

blocks.title: Cycle
blocks.body: Sporophyte (2n) → meiosis → spores (n) → mitosis → gametophyte (n) → gametes and fertilization → zygote (2n) → new sporophyte.

blocks.title: Remember
blocks.body: Meiosis produces spores and reduces chromosome number; mitosis develops the gametophyte; fertilization restores the diploid sporophyte generation.
